name: iterator
intent: Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation, by moving traversal state and the traversal algorithm out of the aggregate into a separate iterator object.
problem: Traversal leaks into every client: code that walks a collection has to know its storage layout (array indices, node links, hash buckets), the same loop is rewritten once per aggregate and once per client, and adding a new traversal order means changing the aggregate's interface — which is exactly what prevents algorithms from being written once and applied to any collection.
context: Applies wherever a collection with a non-trivial or changeable representation must be traversed by outsiders: collection libraries, trees and graphs with several traversal orders, lazy or unbounded sources, and streaming pipelines. It matters most when more than one traversal may be pending at the same time, when the storage must stay hidden for encapsulation or safety, or when traversal algorithms must be added without touching the aggregate; the toolchain only decides which realization is available (a language iteration protocol, generators, lazy sequences, or a hand-written cursor).
benefits: Traversal state lives in the iterator, not the aggregate, so several traversals can be in progress over the same collection independently.
Clients depend on one traversal protocol instead of the storage layout: a single loop or algorithm works over arrays, linked lists, trees and hash tables alike.
New traversal orders arrive as new iterators; the aggregate's interface and existing clients stay closed for modification.
The aggregate's interface stays small and cohesive — it maintains elements, the iterator traverses them — keeping the representation free to change behind the collection's surface.
External iteration can be paused, resumed, passed around and composed across function boundaries, which internal-iteration callbacks (forEach/each) cannot express.
tradeoffs: An extra iterator object (and its allocation and per-element dispatch) per traversal where a plain index loop would cost nothing; the indirection is measurable in hot loops.

The iterator shares the aggregate's storage, so structural modification during traversal invalidates it — ConcurrentModificationException, per-container C++ invalidation rules, Python's RuntimeError on dict resize, or a silently wrong result; only Rust turns that hazard into a compile error.

Cursor semantics are one-shot and stateful, so code that stores or copies an iterator expecting a replayable sequence breaks (Scala's 'never use an iterator after calling a method on it', copied Swift iterators, spent generators).
Laziness defers work until a terminal operation: exceptions surface far from the mistake and re-enumeration recomputes unless the caller materializes the result.

Infinite or very large sequences silently hang consumers that materialize them, and each language's lazy pipeline adds its own footguns (re-evaluation, unconsumed chains, buffered non-streaming operators).
Shared iterator state is not thread-safe: concurrent traversals of a mutable aggregate race unless each traversal owns its cursor and the aggregate defines its concurrency policy.

participants.responsibility: Defines the interface for accessing and traversing elements (hasNext/next, a begin/end pair, an Option-returning next(), or the language's protocol equivalent).
Implements the traversal for one aggregate: keeps the current position and any extra state (index, node pointer, stack, filter predicate) and enforces the end-of-traversal condition.
Defines the operation that creates an iterator (createIterator()/iterator()/makeIterator()/All()) and nothing about the traversal itself.
Implements iterator creation and returns the concrete iterator appropriate to its own storage, so the storage layout stays private to it.
Uses the Iterator and Aggregate interfaces only — it drives the traversal, never the representation, and may hold several iterators at once.

use_cases: Collection libraries that must serve arrays, linked lists, trees, and hash tables through one protocol — e.g. std::begin/end in C++, java.util.Iterator, IEnumerable<T> in C#, Symbol.iterator in JavaScript, IntoIterator in Rust.

Tree and graph APIs exposing depth-first, breadth-first, in-order, or post-order traversal without publishing node links or parent pointers, enabling clients to walk composite structures without coupling to the storage representation.

Lazy or unbounded sources consumed one element at a time: file lines (BufferedReader.lines()), network socket streams, paginated API responses, sensor data, event streams, and generated sequences (random numbers, Fibonacci, permutations).

Streaming data pipelines (map/filter/reduce over any iterable) that stay O(1) in memory regardless of input size, implemented via itertools, Java Stream API, Kotlin Sequence, C++ ranges, Rust iterator adapters, or Go iter package.
Legacy or third-party aggregates whose internal layout must stay private behind a stable traversal interface, allowing the aggregate to refactor its storage without breaking existing clients.
Custom containers that must participate in the language's own for/foreach/for-in/for-await loop, spread operators, destructuring assignment, or list comprehensions.
Database result sets and ORM cursors where the full result set is never materialised in memory; the iterator fetches pages on demand.
Parser and lexer token streams where the input is consumed incrementally and the full source may not fit in memory.

Async I/O pipelines where the iteration protocol yields Promises (JavaScript async generators, C# IAsyncEnumerable<T>, Python async generators) enabling for-await iteration over network responses or file reads.
Multidimensional collection traversal (matrices, nested lists, spatial grids) via flattened iterators that expose a flat index space while hiding the multi-dimensional layout.
Paginated REST or GraphQL API clients where a client-side iterator transparently fetches successive pages as the consumer pulls elements, keeping memory constant regardless of result set size.
Kafka, log-processor, or ETL pipelines where each stage is a transforming iterator: parse → filter → enrich → validate → sink, with each stage evaluated lazily.
Event-driven systems using async iterators to consume WebSocket messages, SSE streams, or queue consumers through a uniform for-await-of interface.
Batch-processing jobs over large file sets (CSV, Parquet, NDJSON) where an iterator wraps a file reader and yields one record per next() call without loading the file into memory.

Cursor-based (keyset) pagination over large, live datasets where offset/limit pagination causes duplicates or missed rows when data is inserted or deleted mid-traversal; the iterator stores the last-seen key rather than a page offset, making traversal stable across concurrent modifications.

Iterator fusion in compilers and runtimes: adjacent map/filter/map chains fused into a single pass with zero intermediate allocation (Rust iterator adapters, Java Spliterators, Haskell stream fusion, C++ range views), giving lazy pipelines near-handwritten performance.

Parallel iterators for data-parallel workloads: Rust Rayon, Java parallel streams, and Kotlin asFlow().buffer() split the iterator across worker threads — identical interface to serial iteration, transparent parallel execution.

Reactive streams bridging pull and push: RxJava, RxJS, and Project Reactor implement backpressure (consumer signals demand, producer emits at requested rate), combining iterator's pull semantics with observer's push delivery.

LLM and streaming AI responses where the model yields tokens incrementally; an async iterator wraps the SSE/stream endpoint and the client consumes tokens one at a time via for-await-of, keeping first-token latency low and enabling progressive rendering.

Cursor-based database driver iterators (Node.js pg cursor, Python asyncpg, Go database/sql rows) where the driver streams rows from the server without loading the full result set, with configurable fetch size controlling server-side memory usage.

Java's Spliterator API exposes a cursor that can be advanced one element at a time or split into subranges for parallel streams; it demonstrates that an iterator contract can include explicit partitioning and size/order characteristics rather than only next().

.NET's IAsyncEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerator<T> expose asynchronous pull iteration through await foreach; GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken) makes cancellation part of the iterator boundary for network, file, and database streams.

WHATWG ReadableStream async iteration lets browser and server consumers use for-await-of over streamed chunks while the iterator locks a reader and defines whether early return() cancels or merely releases it.
avoid_when: A plain index loop over a contiguous buffer, or the language's built-in loop over an array the client already owns, is simpler than introducing an iterator object.
The traversal is a private one-off walk inside the aggregate's own class: a direct loop over the private field is clearer than handing out an iterator to yourself.
The data is a value object or record with no hidden structure and no alternative traversal orders.
The language's pipeline idiom already covers the work (LINQ, Stream, Sequence, comprehensions): use the pipeline instead of building iterators by hand.
Traversal must cross a process or service boundary: return a materialized result or paginate instead of shipping a live cursor (which also creates N+1 access).
anti_patterns: 'Fat aggregate' interfaces that grow first/last/next/previous/max operations instead of handing out iterators, so every new traversal edits the aggregate and the interface grows without bound.

Iterators that reach into the aggregate's internals (friend classes, public fields, raw node pointers), recreating the coupling the pattern exists to remove and making the aggregate's storage layout a public API.
Holding a live cursor across a mutation or a boundary (savepoint, transaction, page navigation) and treating the resulting exception, dangling state, or stale result as normal control flow.

Re-implementing the traversal protocol on top of a language that already dispatches on one — a hand-rolled cursor class in Python, Rust, or Kotlin instead of implementing __iter__/__next__, the Iterator trait, or using a generator.
Using iterator.remove() or in-place mutation during traversal as the primary update path, hiding structural changes inside what looks like a read-only traversal loop.
Returning self as the iterator from a collection's iterator method, making the collection and its iterator the same object — this prevents nested traversals and any re-entrant iteration.

Iterator exhaustion silently swallowing data: passing an already-consumed generator or iterator to two consumers — the second gets zero items with no error — especially dangerous in ETL pipelines where entire datasets disappear without any exception.

Modifying the underlying collection during iteration without using the iterator's own remove/add methods: ConcurrentModificationException in Java, silent data corruption or skipped elements in JavaScript/TypeScript, RuntimeError in Python.
Using for...in instead of for...of in JavaScript/TypeScript, causing iteration over property keys rather than iterable values for custom objects.
Implementing Symbol.iterator but forgetting to return { value, done } correctly, or returning done: true with a value — confusing consumers.
Unbounded prefetching in async iterators: fetching pages or chunks ahead of the consumer without backpressure, causing memory bloat when the consumer is slower than the producer.
design_principles: Encapsulation (information hiding): expose elements and traversal, never the storage.
Single responsibility: the aggregate maintains elements, the iterator traverses them.
Program to an interface: clients depend on the Iterator and Aggregate abstractions, not concrete cursor types.
Open/closed principle: new traversal algorithms are new iterators, not new aggregate methods.
Separation of concerns: the traversal algorithm stays orthogonal to the data structure it walks.
Fail-fast on invariant violations: structural modification during traversal should be detected and signalled, not silently produce wrong results.
best_practices: Expose one creation operation returning the abstract iterator type; keep concrete cursor types private to the aggregate. Prefer the language's factory method or protocol entry point (iterator(), __iter__(), makeIterator(), All()) over public concrete iterators.
Give every traversal its own iterator instance with private cursor state; never keep the cursor on the aggregate — only one traversal at a time prevents independent concurrency and composability.

Define and document the modification policy during traversal (fail-fast, snapshot copy, or explicit invalidation) instead of leaving it undefined; communicate the exact exception or undefined behaviour that results from structural modification mid-iteration.

Implement the native iteration protocol for the target language (Symbol.iterator in JavaScript, __iter__/__next__ in Python, Iterator<T> interface in Java, the Iterator trait in Rust, IEnumerable<T> in C#, Seq/V2 in Go 1.23+) instead of hand-rolling an equivalent from scratch.

Prefer generators or lazy sequences over materialising intermediate collections when composing pipeline stages (map/filter/reduce chains, itertools, Kotlin Sequence, C++ ranges, Rust iterator adapters); measure the cost of each yield when latency matters.

Keep iterators single-pass and cheap; hand callers a collection or a fresh result set when they need to replay or re-enumerate — not a spent cursor or exhausted generator. Follow Scala's rule: never call a method on an iterator after consuming it.

Make laziness explicit in the API: can the sequence be infinite or unbounded, does re-enumeration recompute or return a cached result, and where does the terminal operation execute (CPU, GPU, network, disk)?

Close or dispose resource-holding iterators (database cursors, file handles, network streams) using the language's protocol (return() in JS, __exit__ context manager in Python, Drop trait in Rust, using statement in C#, try-with-resources in Java). Use finally blocks or context managers to guarantee cleanup even on early break.

For composite/tree structures, prefer an explicit Iterator over recursive traversal: the iterator encapsulates the stack or queue for depth-first or breadth-first order, keeping the aggregate interface minimal.

Prefer external iteration with language-native for/foreach/for-in loops over internal callbacks (forEach/each/map in JS) when you need pause, resume, or early termination — external iteration gives the caller control of the loop.
Use bidirectional or random-access iterators only when the underlying storage supports O(1) seek; a bidirectional iterator over a linked list still costs O(n) per step.

Prefer generators over hand-rolled iterator classes when traversal state is simple (position index, stack for tree walk); use explicit iterator classes when traversal state is complex, requires cleanup, or the iterator must expose more than next/hasNext.
Detect accidental iterator reuse in defensive Python code with iter(x) is iter(x) check; raise TypeError if the caller passes an already-exhausted iterator where a container/iterable is expected.
hasNext() must be idempotent: calling it any number of times must not advance the cursor or skip elements.

In async iterators (async generators, IAsyncEnumerable, async function*), always handle cancellation via return()/aclose() in a finally block, and apply backpressure so the producer does not outpace the consumer.

For Java: prefer the enhanced for-each loop (requires Iterable<T>); always call hasNext() before next(); use Iterator.remove() — never collection.remove() — for safe removal during traversal; document whether the iterator is fail-fast, snapshot, or weakly consistent.

For JavaScript/TypeScript: implement both next() returning { value, done } and [Symbol.iterator]() returning this for iterables, or [Symbol.asyncIterator]() returning this for async iterables; never conflate for...in (keys) with for...of (values).
Document iteration order guarantees: for Sets, HashMaps, and concurrent collections the order may be insertion order, hash order, or undefined — clients should not depend on undocumented order.
pitfalls: Iterator exhaustion: Iterators and generators are single-use: once all elements are consumed, calling next() raises StopIteration (Python) or returns {done: true} (JS/TS) indefinitely. Passing an already-exhausted iterator to a second consumer silently yields zero items with no error — particularly insidious in ETL pipelines where entire datasets vanish without exception. Mitigation: Always pass the original iterable (list, generator function, or custom container) to functions that need multiple independent traversals. In defensive Python code, detect iterators with iter(x) is iter(x) and raise TypeError. Call the generator factory function to get a fresh generator on each pass.

ConcurrentModificationException (Java) / structural modification mid-iteration: Modifying an ArrayList, HashMap, or any fail-fast collection via collection.remove/add/clear while an iterator is active causes the iterator's modCount snapshot to diverge from the collection's modCount, throwing ConcurrentModificationException on the next hasNext()/next() call. The same bug silently skips elements or produces wrong results in non-fail-fast collections. Mitigation: Always route structural modifications through the iterator's own remove() (or ListIterator's add()/set()) rather than the collection. For additions (which plain Iterator does not support), use collect-then-apply or ListIterator.add(). Never call collection.remove() inside a for-each loop.

for...in vs for...of (JavaScript/TypeScript): for...in iterates over enumerable property names (keys/indices), not over iterable values. Applying for...in to a custom iterable object iterates over its properties rather than its elements, producing unexpected results. Mitigation: Use for...of for iterating over iterable values; use for...in for iterating over object keys. Ensure custom iterables implement Symbol.iterator and test with for...of.

hasNext() with side effects: An iterator whose hasNext() advances the cursor as a side effect causes callers to skip elements whenever they call hasNext() more than once per iteration step — a common bug when callers write while (it.hasNext()) { it.hasNext(); ... } or when static analysers insert duplicate checks. Mitigation: hasNext() must be idempotent and must not mutate cursor state. Cursor advancement belongs exclusively in next().

Infinite iterator materialisation: Passing an infinite or unbounded iterator (fibonacci(), primes(), random_numbers(), a live WebSocket stream) to list(), [...], collect(), or any terminal operation that materialises the full sequence causes out-of-memory or an infinite hang. Mitigation: Always guard infinite iterators with take(n), limit(n), takeWhile(predicate), or similar at the point of consumption. Document whether an iterator can be infinite.

Missing __iter__ on Python custom iterator: A Python class that implements __next__ but forgets __iter__ cannot be used in for loops, list() constructors, or any tool that calls iter(). The error surfaces as TypeError: object is not iterable, often long after the class was written. Mitigation: Python iterators must implement both __iter__ (returning self for iterator objects) and __next__. Use a generator function instead of a manual class when possible — the generator protocol is harder to misimplement.

Async iterator backpressure: An async generator that prefetches pages or batches ahead of the consumer (e.g., pre-loading multiple API pages into a buffer) without flow-control signalling causes unbounded memory growth when the consumer is slower than the producer. Mitigation: Use bounded queues or explicit flow control in async generators. Use stream.pipeline() in Node.js, which propagates backpressure automatically. Prefer pull-based iteration (consumer requests next()) over push-based prefetching.

Iterator/subclass returned from __iter__: In Python, returning a custom Iterator subclass from __iter__() instead of self or a new instance means the iterable is not reusable: after the first for loop exhausts the returned iterator, subsequent loops either get an exhausted object or fail silently. JavaScript: returning the collection itself from [Symbol.iterator]() prevents nested traversal. Mitigation: Each call to iterator() or __iter__() must return a fresh cursor. A collection (iterable) should return a new iterator; an iterator should return itself. Follow the iter() protocol contract: iter(iter(x)) is iter(x) means x is an iterator, not an iterable.

Iterator protocol mismatch: Returning {done: false, value} after the last element (instead of {done: true}), or returning both done: true and a value, violates the iterator protocol and causes inconsistent behaviour across consumers (for...of ignores the value, explicit .next() may not). Mitigation: Always return {done: true} (and typically value: undefined) as the terminal signal. The value field is ignored when done is true.

Cursor-based pagination instability with offset/limit: Using offset/limit (page number) pagination inside an iterator over a live dataset causes rows to appear twice or be skipped when rows are inserted or deleted between page fetches — the offset drifts from the actual cursor position. Calling the iterator again after a mutation resumes from the wrong position. Mitigation: Use keyset (cursor) pagination: store the last-seen sort key (ID, timestamp, composite key) rather than a page offset. Resume iteration by WHERE sort_key > last_seen_key rather than OFFSET n. This is stable across concurrent inserts and deletions.

Iterator state retained after early break: A for-loop with an early break leaves the iterator positioned at the break point. If the caller or a later code path re-uses the same iterable expecting a fresh traversal, the second loop starts from the break position rather than from the beginning — silently yielding fewer or different elements. Mitigation: Never expose the same iterable object for re-traversal after an early break unless the iterable is explicitly documented as replayable. Create a new iterator for each independent traversal pass.

Silent iterator invalidation on dict/map resize (Python): In Python, iterating over a dict and triggering a resize (by adding enough new keys) raises RuntimeError. But iterating over a dict's view (dict.items(), dict.values()) while the underlying dict is modified only raises RuntimeError if the dict size changes — not when values are mutated in place. This creates inconsistent state depending on the modification type. Mitigation: Prefer iterating over a snapshot (list(dict.items())) when modifications may occur during traversal. Use dict views only when the underlying dict is guaranteed stable for the duration of iteration.

Iterator fusion pipeline re-evaluating expensive operations: Iterator fusion in Rust, Haskell, or C++ ranges can fuse adjacent stages, but re-ordering or fusing stages that have observable side effects (log statements, network calls in a map function, metrics) changes when those side effects fire — potentially causing timeouts, reordered events, or tests that pass or fail non-deterministically depending on fusion decisions. Mitigation: Do not place side-effecting functions inside fused iterator pipelines. Treat map/filter as potentially lazy and fusible; extract side effects to terminal operations or use explicit (non-lazy) intermediate collections when ordering matters.

Early-exit cleanup for resource-backed iterators: Breaking or cancelling an iterator backed by a file, socket, stream reader, or database cursor can leave the resource open when the iterator's close/return/dispose path is not reached or its ownership is unclear. Async iteration makes this easy to miss because cancellation can interrupt an awaited next() before the consumer observes exhaustion. Mitigation: Make iterator lifetime explicit: pair consumption with the language's close protocol (return()/aclose()/DisposeAsync/using), put cleanup in finally, propagate cancellation into the producer, and test break, exception, and cancellation paths.

Parallel splitting changes ordering and reduction semantics: Splittable or parallel iterators may process partitions out of encounter order. A consumer that assumes stable ordering, mutates shared state, or combines partial results with a non-associative operation can produce nondeterministic or numerically different results even though every element was visited. Mitigation: Require ordered traversal or an ordered collector when order matters; use associative, side-effect-free reductions for parallel execution; otherwise keep the iterator sequential and confine each cursor to one worker.

related_patterns_notes.composite: Iterator and Composite cooperate to traverse tree-like hierarchies. The iterator encapsulates the traversal stack (DFS/BFS state), while Composite provides the part-whole hierarchy; together they allow walking a tree without exposing node links to clients. The ITERATOR+COMPOSITE+VISITOR trio is one of the most common pattern combinations in compilers, file browsers, XML/JSON parsers, GUI widget hierarchies, and game scene graphs. The Composite's GetElements() (or equivalent) is the factory method that yields children; the iterator wraps the recursion.
related_patterns_notes.factory-method: Factory Method is the natural companion for creating iterators: the aggregate's createIterator() operation is a factory method that vends the appropriate concrete iterator for the aggregate's current storage representation. This decouples the client from knowing which iterator class to instantiate. In languages with named traversal methods ( breadthFirst(), inOrder() ), each is a named factory method for its concrete iterator.
related_patterns_notes.visitor: Iterator and Visitor are complementary: the iterator controls traversal (which element comes next), while the visitor encapsulates the operation applied at each element. They can be combined (a visitor that holds traversal state) or kept separate (iterator drives walk, visitor provides type-specific apply()). A common design error is conflating them, giving the visitor traversal responsibility or the iterator operation-application responsibility. The ITERATOR+COMPOSITE+VISITOR triad is particularly powerful for AST processing: Composite structures the tree, Iterator walks it, Visitor applies transformations.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Iterator can use Strategy internally: the traversal algorithm (depth-first vs breadth-first, recursive vs iterative) can be parameterised as a Strategy object injected into the concrete iterator, making traversal order swappable without changing the aggregate. The iterator itself becomes a Strategy context. Strategy also governs filter predicates and transformation functions passed to filtering or mapping iterators.
related_patterns_notes.memento: Memento captures iterator state (position, visited flags, stack) to support snapshot-and-resume or undo of a traversal. This is particularly useful in editors and parsers where you may need to checkpoint a walk and restore it after an edit, or in search UIs where a user can step back through previous result pages.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Template Method defines the skeleton of a traversal algorithm in the aggregate or base iterator class, deferring concrete steps (child visitation order, filtering) to subclasses. C++ STL algorithms use this hybrid with Functors. The base iterator's next() implements the skeleton; concrete subclasses override node-access hooks.
related_patterns_notes.generator: A generator is a language-specific lightweight realisation of the Iterator pattern: it automatically suspends and resumes execution state using yield, eliminating the need for an explicit cursor class. Generators in Python (yield), JavaScript (function* + yield), C# (yield return), and Go 1.23+ (range-over-function) are the idiomatic way to implement iterators in those languages. A generator function returns a fresh iterator object each time it is called; a generator variable holds a one-shot cursor.
related_patterns_notes.collection-pipeline: Collection Pipeline (functional-style map/filter/reduce chains) is often built on top of iterators: each pipeline stage receives and produces an iterator or iterable, keeping the entire pipeline lazy and O(1) in memory. Rust's iterator adapters (`.filter().map().take()`), Python's itertools, Kotlin's Sequences, and Java's Stream API are all iterators + collection pipeline in practice. Martin Fowler's PoEAA catalogue treats collection pipeline as a corollary of Iterator.
related_patterns_notes.observer: Iterator and Observer are push/pull duals: Iterator is pull-based (client requests next element), Observer is push-based (source pushes elements to subscribers). Reactive streams (RxJava, RxJS, Project Reactor) bridge both — they are pull-based on the consumer side but push-based on the producer side. Async iterables can model event streams where Observer would otherwise be used.
related_patterns_notes.repository: Repository pattern (PoEAA) can be implemented on top of an iterator for paginated data sources: the repository returns an iterator that transparently fetches pages on demand from a REST API, database, or search engine, keeping the client interface uniform while the pagination mechanism stays private.
